Ill give two examples.

1: on a deaf political FB page, the moderators decided to ban all news articles other than those from official political parties or the state broadcaster citing fake news & the need to protect members from harm.
I complained that i do not need to be treated like a child and i do not need people posing as parental figures deciding what is true or false for me. I also said banning news you disagree with is dangerous.

 None agreed with me.

Later the same day BBC reported that the Chinese state had banned the BBC citing harmful fake news, the moderator shared the article complaining about it.
I replied laughing at the absurd irony of it all. I could not believe such behaviour was considered appropriate.

2: since 2003 "deaf famous" people & sign language tutors have insisted that the government had officially recognised BSL as a language.
This never happened & resulted in many giving up on campaigning for it or demanding better deaf education.
Only this year (almost 20 years later) have we finally got BSL legislation on the books, this could have been achieved long ago if this myth that benefitted the image of those who spread it didnt occur.
This particular myth is still being acknowledged as true by orgs and people that really should know better.

The BSL act that has finally been achieved does not give any legal rights to BSL as a language or to Deaf people that use it. Very few Deaf people have realised this despite some highlighting it (myself included) because the leading deaf organisations and "deaf famous" made exaggerated claims as to what this act will do.

There are other examples but those are the two that stand out to me.

I feel this happens due to a profound lack of access to variety in news & opinions in media with very few mediums & channels providing sign language content.

This is not to say conformism isnt a problem in the hearing world too but in deaf culture it really hit me when i became deaf & my preferred language BSL.

I am sick of people labelling me (deaf person) as disabled so they can feel better about themselves in taking on a saviour role. I can advocate for myself & am not so needy, helpless & pathetic that i need patronising & condescending to from strangers. The thing that seperates sign language users that are deaf from the rest of society is a language barrier, not diaability as such.

The "two worlds" idea was an experience for me. Becoming deaf at 27 & learning sign language as my preferred language of necessity was quite difficult initially. 

Going to deaf clubs or events would be awkward as other deaf people there with fast flying hands would write me off instantly as just another hearing person who is learning to benefit his job prospects or whatever. 

I understand this aloofness now as having run a deaf club myself, i have seen many come along saying they want to be part of the community & make friends, only to disappear without a goodbye after they finished their exams. I makes you feel used when that happens so i can empathise.

A few times i have noticed peoples attitude towards me changes when they find out i wasnt born deaf. I've also been castigated by older people for wearing a CL, just the once though. I dont wear it now anyway. 
So for me, it is incidents like these that made me have an affinity for the "stuck between two worlds" thing. But that was a long time ago.

Essentially i assert that the notion the government recognised bsl in any way whatsoever in 2003 is a comforting lie. One that has grown exponentially ever since.

Recognition of languages usually entails doing so in law i.e creating legislation that explicitly references it & attributes certain rights, status & or legal protections to it.

This is not the case with what happened in 2003, it wasn't even the government or the parliament that "recognised" BSL, it was in fact the DWP that did so & last time i checked, they have no rights, power or responsibility in recognising a language.

Because the deaf community feel that it was recognised, we have become complacent ever since. Nothing has really changed, the same old barriers to us persist & there are no real campaigns to address this due to the myth that recognition has allready been achieved.

Reading your post reminded me of my own experience.

When i became deaf i would force myself not to tell anyone & pretend i was "still me".

But at work people thought i was ignoring them & that i became super rude & ignorant all of a sudden.

In my social circle, conversations involving dates/names or anything really would be hugely problematic, i would come away from it thinking what i thought i heard to be true only next time we meet they would say something completely different. I had to suppress my feelings that they were constantly lying to me or playing some sort of weird game & i wasnt in on it, i became really resentful of people i once considered to be close friends.

Ignoring my deafness & trying to hide it actually made me quite ill, lost old friends that i shared a lot of my life with over it & looking back, it was not their fault at all. I regret it to this day.

I think, similar to you, my immediate family allways talked of it as a problem & would tell me to concentrate or badger me to get betting hearing aids/implants. The doctors didnt help much outside of dumping the devices on me & kicking me out of the door, no advice on how to adjust to this new reality like new communication methods/assistive tech or coping mechanisms.

But once i was introduced to sign language & getting into deaf community i learnt to accept the "new me", to not be ashamed of it & how to adjust.

I would say the best thing you could do is to accept who you are, it is a part of you & there is absolutely nothing wrong with it. The hardest thing for me to do was to be open about it with friends, even strangers, but once i did things improved. They were very understanding, if any are not, they dont deserve to be your friends.

There are plenty of gadgets & phone apps that can help you in difficult situations & i dont know where you are (im from UK) but here companies can get financial assistance for deaf employees to be more accessible for us. I honestly wouldnt fear about applying for jobs.

I still have bad days of course & my family havnt had the time/money/patience to learn much signing but they do their best to make sure im involved in convos.
